q-210742:
Let's set $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\cdot 3{x}^{2}=\frac{3}{x}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{6\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})}{x}\,\text{d}x & =6\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x}\cdot  \\  & =6\int u\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{6}{3}\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & ={u}^{2}+C \\  & ={ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-31329:
Let $u={log}_{2}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{2}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {log}_{2}⁡x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\int u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\cdot \frac{{log}_{2}^{2}⁡x}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-31401:
Let $u={log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2}).$Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\,⟹\,\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {log}_{3}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\int u\cdot (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}\int u\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3{log}_{3}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-13845:
Let's set $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4x}\cdot 4=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives the following:

| $x$ | $1$ | $e/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡4$ | $1$ |

We now substitute and evaluate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e/4}\frac{1}{4x\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{e/4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4x)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{1}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|){|}_{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(0-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡4)\end{aligned}
$$

q-73664:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=5-2{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=6{x}^{2}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{x}^{2}{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}\cdot 6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot \,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-{e}^{5-2{x}^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-113847:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=4-{x}^{4}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,-2\text{d}u=8{x}^{3}\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 8{x}^{3}{e}^{4-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{4-{x}^{4}}\cdot 8{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-2)\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-2{e}^{4-{x}^{4}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-73801:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={x}^{2}+1.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x{6}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {6}^{{x}^{2}+1}\cdot 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {6}^{u}\cdot \,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{6}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C \\  & =\frac{{6}^{{x}^{2}+1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-31420:
Let's introduce the new variable $u=3{x}^{2}.$ Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{8}^{3{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int {8}^{3{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {8}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int {8}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\frac{{8}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C \\  & =\frac{{8}^{3{x}^{2}}}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-31478:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u={5}^{x}+1.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={5}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡5\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u={5}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{5}^{x}}{{5}^{x}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{5}^{x}+1}\cdot {5}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|{5}^{x}+1|+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({5}^{x}+1)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that ${5}^{x}+1>0$ for all $x.$

q-31480:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we introduce the new variable $u={4}^{x}+2.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={4}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡4\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,\text{d}u={4}^{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{4}^{x}}{{4}^{x}+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{4}^{x}+2}\cdot {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|{4}^{x}+2|+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡({4}^{x}+2)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, in the last step, we used the fact that ${4}^{x}+2>0$ for all $x.$

q-114288:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 4x{e}^{8x}\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=4 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{8x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{8}{e}^{8x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 4x\cdot {e}^{8x}\,\text{d}x & =4x\cdot \frac{1}{8}{e}^{8x}-\int \frac{1}{8}{e}^{8x}\cdot 4\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x{e}^{8x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}x{e}^{8x}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{8x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{x{e}^{8x}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{8x}}{16}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-12560:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int (x+7){e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x+7\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{2x+5}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int (x+7)\cdot {e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =(x+7)\cdot \frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\int \frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{2}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x+7){e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{(x+7){e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2x+5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(x+7){e}^{2x+5}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2x+5}}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-74090:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int 10x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=10x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=10 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int 10x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =10x\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))\cdot 10\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 10x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =10x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-10\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =10x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+10\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-114314:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x=uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\int x{csc}^{2}⁡x\text{d}x$ as $\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x.$ Therefore we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={csc}^{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=-\operatorname{cot}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ where $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{csc}^{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-x\operatorname{cot}⁡x+\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-49674:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⇒ & v=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}-{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x){|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})]+\frac{1}{4}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{4}]+\frac{1}{4}[0-0] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[0]+0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49660:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-x} & ⇒ & v=-{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot (-{e}^{-x})-\int (-{e}^{-x})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{0}x{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & =-x{e}^{-x}{|}_{-2}^{0}+{\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x{e}^{-x}{|}_{-2}^{0}-{e}^{-x}{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =[-0{e}^{-0}-2{e}^{2}]-[{e}^{0}-{e}^{2}] \\  & =-2{e}^{2}-1+{e}^{2} \\  & =-1-{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
